1.explanation: All of the D-language syntax rules live in components/prism-d.js, in particular the array of regexes under the 'string' key. Those patterns are responsible for matching both single‐quoted chars and double/backtick‐quoted strings. The final regex (/(['`])(?:\\[\s\S]|(?!\1)[^\\])*\1[cwd]?/) is intended to match double‐quoted and backtick‐quoted strings but fails when a single‐quote appears inside a double‐quoted string, so the highlighter terminates the string too early. Adjusting this regex (or introducing a more precise pattern for embedded quotes) in prism-d.js is required to fix the bug.
1.bug_scenario: When highlighting D-language source, embedding a single‐quote character inside a normal double‐quoted string (e.g. "It’s") causes Prism to break out of the string token early, leaving the closing quote and rest of the text un-highlighted or mis-colored. Backtick‐quoted (WYSIWYG) strings work correctly, but normal double-quoted strings do not tolerate an apostrophe.

2.explanation: In the D grammar (components/prism-d.js) the 'string' token is defined as an array of regexes. The character-literal regex /'(?:\\'|\\?[^']+)'/ is too broad (it can match more than one character and doesn’t guard against embedded single quotes inside a double-quoted context), and the final fallback regex for quoted strings/backtick strings also doesn’t stop at a single quote when inside double quotes. As a result, "It’s" is split into "It" (string), s" (extra), breaking the intended syntax highlighting. Adjusting these two patterns so that only valid single-character literals match the char rule and so that single quotes don’t terminate a double-quoted string will restore correct highlighting.
2.bug_scenario: On the PrismJS test page with D-language highlighting, putting a single quote inside a double-quoted string (e.g. "It’s") causes the highlighter to think the string ends at the single quote. Everything after that point is mis-colored. Backtick-quoted strings work correctly, but the D grammar’s own string/character rules are too permissive and don’t prevent that premature closure.
